newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysian markets tripped up by falling ring.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysian markets tripped up by falling ring.

text.p: A storm rocking Malaysia's financial markets turned ferocious on Monday, hammering the already beleaguered currency to a 42-month low and the key stocks index to a 21-month nadir low.

The ringgit lost another two percent to 2.74 per dollar, taking its month-long fall to nearly 10 percent, and the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index ended 3.24 percent lower at 902.14, just above the key 900-point psychological barrier.

But commodity prices -- palm oil and tin -- rallied on hopes that a weak ringgit would boost export earnings. Malaysia's benchmark palm oil October futures contract closed 20 ringgit higher at 1,220 ringgit ($446.07) a tonne and tin rose to a 5-1/2-month high of 14.70 ringgit per kg.
Analysts and dealers said foreign funds again led the dramatic downward slide in the stock and currency markets.

Malaysian authorities stayed on the sidelines following remarks by Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on Friday that Malaysia was satisfied with the ringgit's level and would not let speculators profit by trying to prop up the currency.
"I thought we had seen the worst, but today is quite bad on all fronts," said Sani Hamid, economist with MMS International in Singapore.
"I think it was the PM's comments (on Friday) that triggered the selling of the ringgit. He added to the bearishness."
The currency plunged nearly two percent on Friday and has remained under pressure since.
Analysts said Mahathir's remarks were taken to mean that the central Bank Negara Malaysia would not intervene to stop the local unit from being sold.

"This was the last thing that the ringgit needed, given (that) regional currency woes (were) still pretty much unresolved, thus opening the way to more ringgit downside," research house I.D.E.A. said in a Monday morning commentary.
Sani of MMS said the stocks index and ringgit were getting dangerously close to their lowest levels this decade.
The ringgit's lowest level since 1990 is 2.80 per dollar reached in July 1991 and for the Composite Index it is 836 points in January 1995, he said.
"All hell's breaking loose," said a dealing manager at a local brokerage. "It seems like foreigners want to get out of the ringgit."
"Almost everybody agrees that 880 is the next support level (for the index). There is only limited support around 900.
"There is a lot of foreign selling, but the rest is forced selling, including some selling by banks and even the local funds on their clients shares held as collateral," said the dealing manager.

Hugh Young, managing director of Aberdeen Asset Management in Singapore, said the selling was mainly due to exchange rate uncertainty, "elements of a bubble economy", and borrowing for the construction of large infrastructure projects.
Lack of a clear policy during the current currency crisis was another reason for the continuing attack on Malaysian financial markets, analysts said.

"I think hedge funds (selling the currency) are encouraged by the fact that Malaysia does not have a well thought-out policy on the ringgit," said Danial Lian, regional economist with NatWest Markets in Singapore.
He cited contradictory statements by Mahathir and half-hearted policy moves by the government.
Dealers said they were surprised by Mahathir's remarks on Friday, following his recent stinging verbal attacks on speculators and the introduction of capital control measures.

Bank Negara last week introduced its first capital control measure in three years, ordering local banks to limit non-trade-related currency swaps to $2.0 million with each overseas customer, in an attempt to reduce foreigners access to the ringgit.
